summary: Defines the Capabilities optional parameter for BGP-4, which lets two peers announce which new features they support when a session starts. This allows new features to be introduced gracefully without tearing down peering sessions. It obsoletes RFC 3392.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5492 lets BGP routers list supported features in the OPEN message that starts a peering. A feature can be used when both routers advertise it, while an unknown capability is ignored instead of ending the session.

subtitle: How BGP peers advertise optional features when they open a session.

tldr.problem: The original BGP-4 rules require a speaker to end a peering when an OPEN message contains an unknown Optional Parameter, making it difficult to add capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: A Capabilities Optional Parameter in OPEN lists capabilities as code, length and value fields. Peers use a capability only when both advertised it, and ignore capabilities they do not recognize.
tldr.outcome: BGP features can be introduced without ending a session simply because a peer does not recognize an optional capability. RFC 5492 obsoletes RFC 3392 and is updated by RFC 8810.

today: RFC 5492 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 3392. It has been updated by RFC 8810.

sections.title: Why BGP Needs Capability Advertisement
sections.content:
The base BGP-4 specification requires a speaker to end a peering if it receives an OPEN message containing an unrecognized Optional Parameter. That rule makes it difficult to introduce new BGP features without disrupting existing peers.

RFC 5492 defines a Capabilities Optional Parameter and rules for processing it. Peers can establish a session even if one does not recognize a listed capability, provided the capabilities needed for the peering are supported.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP routers need a way to describe optional features without causing older peers to disconnect. This RFC puts that information in the session-opening message.

sections.title: How Peers Agree on Capabilities
sections.content:
A speaker that supports capability advertisement may include a Capabilities Optional Parameter in its OPEN message. Each speaker learns the peer's capabilities from the OPEN message it receives.

A capability can be used only if both peers advertised it. If a peer sends a capability the receiver does not recognize, the receiver must ignore it and must not send an Unsupported Capability notification or terminate the session for that reason.

If a peer rejects the Capabilities parameter itself with an Unsupported Optional Parameter notification, the sender should try to establish the BGP connection again without that parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router lists the features it supports, and they use only features on both lists. A router ignores feature codes it does not recognize.

sections.title: The Capabilities Parameter
sections.content:
The Capabilities Optional Parameter has Parameter Type 2. It contains one or more capability entries, each made of a one-octet Capability Code, a one-octet Capability Length and a variable-length Capability Value interpreted according to the code.

A speaker should not include duplicate entries with the same code, length and value, but must be ready to receive them. Multiple instances of one code with different values are allowed when the specification for that capability explains their meaning.

The parameter should normally appear once in OPEN, containing all capabilities. For backward compatibility, speakers must accept multiple Capabilities parameters and process their contents as one set.
sections.plainLanguage: Each capability has a code, a length and a value. Routers normally put all capabilities in one parameter, but must accept them split across several parameters.

sections.title: When a Required Capability Is Missing
sections.content:
RFC 5492 defines the Unsupported Capability notification subcode with value 7. Its Data field lists the capability or capabilities that caused the speaker to send it, encoded as they would be in OPEN.

A speaker may send this notification and end the peering if a capability is required for that session, such as support for exchanging IPv6 routes. The choice is local to the speaker, and the RFC says that such a peering should not be re-established automatically.

The notification must not be sent merely because the speaker received a capability it does not understand. Unknown capabilities are ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: A router may end a peering when it needs a capability the other router lacks. It must not end the peering just because it sees a capability it does not know.

sections.title: IANA Capability Numbers
sections.content:
IANA maintains the Capability Code registry. Code 0 is reserved; codes 1 through 63 use IETF Review; codes 64 through 127 use First Come First Served; and codes 128 through 255 are for Private Use.

IANA also maintains the BGP OPEN Optional Parameter Types registry. Type 0 is reserved, type 1 is the deprecated Authentication parameter and type 2 is Capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the official number lists for capability codes and OPEN parameter types. The allocation rules reserve some ranges for review, private use or later assignment.

sections.title: Security and Changes from RFC 3392
sections.content:
The RFC says capability advertisement does not change the security issues inherent in BGP and points to RFC 4272 for those issues.

Compared with RFC 3392, this document makes editorial changes, updates references, clarifies notification handling and behavior when the Capabilities parameter appears more than once, and changes some recommendations into requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Capability advertisement does not change BGP's underlying security issues. This version clarifies how peers handle notifications and repeated capability parameters.
